rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Likewise” may introduce an omitted subject referring to Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s described journeys and deeds, magnifying him, or his authority among these people as among those at sunset.
rows.anchor: خبر مبتدأ محذوف أي أمر ذي القرنين ذلك والمشار إليه ما وصف به قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it modifies an omitted verbal noun for finding the sun rise, making the experience parallel to finding it set in a muddy spring.
rows.anchor: صفة مصدر محذوف لوجد أي وجدها تطلع وجدانا كوجدانها تغرب في عين حمئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may instead modify an omitted verbal noun for making, or “screen,” or “people,” describing a screen or people like those at sunset.
rows.anchor: صفة مصدر محذوف لنجعل أي لم نجعل لهم سترا جعلا كائنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parse makes “likewise” the object of “reached”: he reached the place of sunrise as he had reached the place of sunset.
rows.anchor: أي ( بلغ ) مغربها كما بلغ مطلعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God comprehensively knows Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s forces, equipment, and means of rule, both outwardly and inwardly; this can magnify the scale of his enterprise.
rows.anchor: من الجنود والآلات وأسباب الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Depending on the earlier parse, the statement may mean God knew what Dhu’l-Qarnayn endured during the journey or the means that brought him to this remote place.
rows.anchor: وقد أحطنا بما لاقاه وحصل له في أثناء سيره خبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings of the clause emphasize Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s good reception and effective conduct, or affirm that the scene was real as it appeared, though its full reality is known only to God.
rows.anchor: أحطنا بما لديه من حسن التلقي وجودة العمل خبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu’l-Qarnayn followed a third route, crossing between east and west from the sunrise region toward the north.
rows.anchor: طريقا ثالثا معترضا بين المشرق والمغرب آخذا من مطلع الشمس إلى الشمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two barriers are mountains; “barrier” applies because they block a mountain pass, though adjacency was also proposed as the basis for the name.
rows.anchor: السد الجبل والحاجز وإطلاق السد عليه لأنه سد فجا من الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Abu Bakr, and Yaʿqub read the word with a damma on sīn; al-Kisaʾi treats both readings as identical in meaning.
rows.anchor: نافع وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي وأبو بكر ويعقوب بضم السين والمعنى على ما قال الكسائي واحد

rows.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
rows.claim: They distinguish the damma form as a noun from the fatha form as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: السد بالضم الاسم وبالفتح المصدر

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: He says the damma form denotes what the eyes see, while the fatha form denotes what they do not see.
rows.anchor: الأول ما رأته عيناك والثاني ما لا تريانه

rows.speaker: عكرمة وأبو عمرو بن العلاء وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: They assign the damma form to a natural barrier made by God and the fatha form to one made by human craft; the author finds both readings compatible with both ideas.
rows.anchor: الأول ما كان من خلق الله تعالى لا دخل لصنع البشر فيه والثاني ما كان لصنع البشر دخل فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reverse the natural-versus-human distinction between the readings, but the author calls that reversal plainly weak and says both readings can agree.
rows.anchor: والمتبادر منه ما فعله العباد وضعفه ظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Between” is parsed as the direct object of “reached”; alternatively it is an adverb with the object, what he sought, omitted.
rows.anchor: على المفعولية لأنه مبلوغ وهو من الظروف المتصرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author locates the barriers near latitude ninety north, associating the northern Gog and Magog account in Ezekiel with the region; Kâtip Çelebi leaned this way.
rows.anchor: وهذان السدان فيما يقرب من عرض تسعين من جهة الشمال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A competing identification places the two mountains in Armenia and Azerbaijan, an identification the author associates with al-Baydawi’s presentation.
rows.anchor: هما جبلا أرمينية وأذربيجان ونسب ذلك إلى ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects identifying the barrier with the famous Darial pass wall: historians attribute it to Anushirwan or Isfandiyar, and it had fallen long before the author’s time.
rows.anchor: فإن باني ذلك السد عندهم كسرى أنو شروان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that the wall and Gog and Magog remain there invisibly, as the Kashfiyya leader Kazim Rashti asserted, is called nonsense and a sign of misguidance.
rows.anchor: وزعم أن السد ويأجوج ومأجوج هناك وأن الكل قد تلطف بحيث لا يرى

rows.speaker: ابن سعيد
rows.claim: He gives the site as longitude 163°, latitude 40°; the author objects that the region is China, its large wall is elsewhere, and its scale and builder do not fit the account.
rows.anchor: إن ذلك الموضع حيث الطول مائة وثلاثة وستون درجة والعرض أربعون درجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possibility is an unknown region; uncharted land or sea may intervene, and failure to find a place does not prove it does not exist.
rows.anchor: هما بموضع من الأرض لا نعلمه وكم فيها من أرض مجهولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since a truthful prophetic report affirms the barriers and related events as possible, believers must accept it as they accept other reports of possible things.
rows.anchor: وبعد إخبار الصادق بوجود هذين السدين وما يتبعهما يلزمنا الإيمان بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some identify the people as Turks; another says they were jinn, a claim the author calls false while allowing it is not impossible, as Abu Hayyan says.
rows.anchor: قيل هم الترك وزعم بعضهم أن القوم كانوا من الجان وهو زعم باطل لا بعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their difficulty understanding speech likely reflects an unusually remote language and limited discernment; the author prefers the ordinary, literal sense of “speech.”
rows.anchor: والظاهر إبقاء القول على معناه المتبادر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari is said to take the phrase figuratively for understanding generally, including gesture and similar communication, with difficulty.
rows.anchor: أي لا يكادون يفهمونه إلا بجهد ومشقة مع إشارة ونحوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author questions that reading and the rule that negating “almost” affirms the action with difficulty; he says that rule is not the preferred analysis.
rows.anchor: وليس بالمختار

rows.speaker: الأعمش وابن أبي ليلى وخلف وابن عيسى الأصبهاني وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Their active-form reading means the people could hardly make others understand them because they stammered and did not articulate letters clearly.
rows.anchor: قرأ الأعمش وابن أبي ليلى وخلف وابن عيسى الأصبهاني وحمزة والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people may have spoken through an interpreter, making the attribution of speech to all of them figurative; Ibn Masʿud’s codex supports this possibility.
rows.anchor: أي بواسطة مترجمهم فإسناد القول إليهم مجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, they may have spoken directly because God gave Dhu’l-Qarnayn the means to understand and communicate with them, or other nearby people may have spoken without translating.
rows.anchor: أو بالذات على أن يكون فهم ذي القرنين كلامهم وإفهامه إياهم

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Gog and Magog are two tribes descended from Japheth, son of Noah; Wahb and many later scholars adopt this genealogy.
rows.anchor: قبيلتان من ولد يافث بن نوح عليه السلام وبه جزم وهب بن منبه

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi’s genealogy has Japheth travel east and father five sons; Achar’s descendants include Gog, Magog, and their peoples, while other sons father Slavs, Romans, Persians, Turks, and Greeks.
rows.anchor: إن يافث سار إلى المشرق فولد له هناك خمسة أولاد

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Another account makes both Gog and Magog part of the Turks.
rows.anchor: كلاهما من الترك وروي ذلك عن الضحاك

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: A report says a Turkish force was a detachment of Gog and Magog that escaped when Dhu’l-Qarnayn built the barrier.
rows.anchor: من طريق السدي من أثر قوى الترك سرية من سرايا يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says there were twenty-two tribes: the wall enclosed twenty-one, while one tribe remained away on a raid and was called the Turks.
rows.anchor: أن يأجوج ومأجوج ثنتان وعشرون قبيلة بنى ذو القرنين السد على إحدى وعشرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported identifications divide Gog and Magog between the Turks and Dailam, or between the Turks and the Jil.
rows.anchor: يأجوج من الترك ومأجوج من الديلم وقيل من الجيل

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb reports that they descended from Adam without Eve, formed from his semen after a nocturnal emission fell into the soil; al-Nawawi says most scholars held this.
rows.anchor: أن يأجوج ومأجوج من ولد آدم عليه السلام من غير حواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defenders of Kaʿb’s story answer that prophets may have nocturnal emissions with their wives or emission without dreaming of intercourse, and that not everyone holds the Flood was universal.
rows.anchor: فيجوز أن يحتلموا بنسائهم فلعل احتلام آدم عليه السلام من القسم الجائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author personally dismisses the Eve-less descent account as a fabulous tale.
rows.anchor: وأنا أرى هذا القول حديث خرافة

rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Hajar says only Kaʿb transmitted the account from the early authorities and cites a Prophetic report placing Gog and Magog among Noah’s descendants.
rows.anchor: لم يرد ذلك على أحد من السلف إلا عن كعب الأحبار ويرده الحديث المرفوع

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A weak marfuʿ report traces Arabs, Persians, and Romans to Shem; Copts, Berbers, and Sudanese to Ham; and Gog, Magog, Turks, and Slavs to Japheth.
rows.anchor: ولد لنوح سام وحام ويافث فولد لسام العرب وفارس والروم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the Jewish claim that Magog is only the land where Gog lived, since the text presents both as tribes.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعض اليهود أن مأجوج اسم للأرض التي كان يسكنها يأجوج وليس اسما لقبيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names are probably foreign proper nouns; if Arabic, they have proposed derivations from rapid movement, fire, heat, or bitter water, with hamza forms read by ʿAsim, al-Aʿmash, and Yaʿqub.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنهما اسمان أعجميان فمنع صرفهما للعلمية والعجمة

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: If the initial hamza is original, al-Akhfash parses Yajuj on the yaʿful pattern and Majuj on mafʿul, deriving them from the blaze of fire.
rows.anchor: إن جعلنا ألفهما أصلية فيأجوج يفعول ومأجوج مفعول كأنه من أجيج النار

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub offers alternative non-hamza derivations from roots meaning to flow or surge.
rows.anchor: في غير الهمز مأجوج فاعول من المج ويأجوج فاعول من من اليج

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن علي بن عبد الصمد السخاوي
rows.claim: Al-Sakhawi regards the names as Arabic with original hamza, then softened; he derives them from tumult, rapid running, heat, or bitter water.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه عربي وأصله الهمز وتركه على التخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Arabic, the names are proper nouns and feminine by tribal reference, which prevents declension.
rows.anchor: وعلة منع الصرف على القول بعربيتهما العلمية والتأنيث باعتبار القبيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAjjaj and his son Ruʾya read Ājūj with hamza instead of yāʾ; non-Qurʾanic usage also has Jūj without either.
rows.anchor: بهمزة بدل الياء وربما يقال جوج بلا همزة ولا ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their corruption includes killing, destruction, and other familiar harms; another view says they seize and consume provisions, while a report says they eat people.
rows.anchor: في أرضنا بالقتل والتخريب وسائر وجوه الإفساد المعلوم من البشر

rows.speaker: حبيب الأوصافي
rows.claim: He says their corruption consisted of eating people.
rows.anchor: كان فسادهم أنهم يأكلون الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their plural description does not establish that Arabic’s smallest plural can be two.
rows.anchor: واستدل بإسناد مفسدون إلى يأجوج ومأجوج على أن أقل الجمع اثنان وليس بشيء أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kharj and kharaj both mean payment here; they may differ as verbal noun versus noun, one-time versus recurring payment, voluntary gift versus obligatory due, or in specificity.
rows.anchor: وقيل الخرج المال يخرج مرة والخراج الخرج المتكرر وقيل الخرج ما تبرعت به

rows.speaker: الحسن والأعمش وطلحة وخلف وابن سعدان وابن عيسى الأصبهاني وابن جبير الأنطاكي وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read kharajan with an added alif; both forms can mean the same thing, as naw and nawal do.
rows.anchor: قرأ الحسن والأعمش وطلحة وخلف وابن سعدان وابن عيسى الأصبهاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assimilated reading of “enabled me” contrasts with Ibn Kathir’s and Humayd’s unassimilated reading; God established him as powerful in rule, wealth, and resources.
rows.anchor: بالإدغام وقرأ ابن كثير وحميد بالفك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What God granted is better than the payment offered, so Dhu’l-Qarnayn has no need of their money.
rows.anchor: مما تريدون أن تبذلوه إلي من الخرج فلا حاجة بي إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Help me with strength” can request useful tools such as iron, people, or both; the command follows from his divine endowment or his refusal of payment.
rows.anchor: بما يتقوى به على المقصود من الآلات كزبر الحديد أو من الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Between you and them” puts the addressed people first to show care for their interests, matching their own phrasing.
rows.anchor: تقديم إضافة الظرف إلى ضمير المخاطبين على إضافته إلى ضمير يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A radm is a compact, strong barrier, stronger than a sadd; the word can denote patching a breach with stones or filling gaps generally.
rows.anchor: حاجزا حصينا وحجابا متينا وهو أكبر من السد وأوثق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls it “the strongest of barriers,” supporting the stronger sense and implying Dhu’l-Qarnayn promises more than requested.
rows.anchor: هو كأشد الحجاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zubar are large pieces of iron; the root conveys gathering, as in assembling letters into a book or the gathered mane of a lion.
rows.anchor: جمع زبرة كغرف في غرفة وهي القطعة العظيمة وأصل الزبر الاجتماع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas defines zubar al-hadid as pieces; Kaʿb ibn Malik’s poetry uses the word of iron and stone.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أن نافع بن الأزرق سأله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Requesting the iron does not contradict refusing payment: they may pay for it or merely carry it over, and tools can be lent without becoming compensation.
rows.anchor: طلب إيتاء الزبر لا ينافي أنه لم يقبل منهم شيئا

rows.speaker: أبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: His reading connects radman to “bring me,” meaning they should bring the iron pieces; iron is singled out because it is crucial and scarce.
rows.anchor: قراءة أبي بكر عن عاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The building action is elided: they supplied the iron and Dhu’l-Qarnayn built incrementally until the structure matched the mountain flanks in height.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا جعل ما بين جانبي الجبلين من البنيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the dam itself is the subject of “matched”; ṣadaf is a mountain’s side, a relational term for facing slopes, while Abu ʿUbayda’s “any lofty building” is not intended.
rows.anchor: لا يقال للمنفرد صدف حتى يصادفه الآخر

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والزهري ومجاهد والحسن
rows.claim: They read ṣadafayn with both consonants rounded; the author says this is Himyari usage, whereas opening both is Tamimi.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والزهري ومجاهد والحسن

rows.speaker: أبو بكر وابن محصين وأبو رجاء وأبو عبد الرحمن
rows.claim: They read the first consonant rounded and the second still; further reported variants include both still, and the two other vowel combinations.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو بكر وابن محصين وأبو رجاء وأبو عبد الرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Blow” addresses the workers with bellows; making the iron fire-hot is a vivid simile, and assigning the act to Dhu’l-Qarnayn highlights his leadership over the workers.
rows.anchor: أي بالكيران في زبر الحديد الموضوعة بين الصدفين ففعلوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the iron was heated, he asked the copper handlers—or, on another reading, the blowers—to bring copper for him to pour over it.
rows.anchor: الذين يتولون أمر النحاس من الإذابة وغيرها وقيل لأولئك النافخين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction deletes the object of “bring” supplied by “pour”; Basran grammarians cite this as evidence that the second verb governs in verb competition.
rows.anchor: فحذف من الأول لدلالة الثاني عليه وبه تمسك البصريون على أن إعمال الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most identify qitr as molten copper; lead and molten iron are alternatives the author deems unsound. A hamzat-wasl reading means “bring it,” summoning hands-on help.
rows.anchor: النحاس المذاب وهو قول الأكثرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common shortened form drops the tāʾ to ease adjacent similar emphatic and dental consonants; readers differ over assimilation, changing sīn to ṣād, or retaining the tāʾ.
rows.anchor: بحذف تاء الافتعال تخفيفا وحذرا عن تلاقي المتقاربين في المخرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once copper was poured over the heated iron, the materials fused into a hard mass; Gog and Magog could neither climb its height and smoothness nor bore through its thickness.
rows.anchor: فاختلط والتصق بعضه ببعض فصار جبلا صلدا فجاء يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports put the wall’s height at 200 or 1,800 cubits and its width at fifty; they describe foundations reaching water and iron laid above rock and copper.
rows.anchor: كان ارتفاعه مائتي ذراع وقيل : ألف وثمانمائة ذراع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immense length and heat of the work would require divine intervention beyond ordinary means, unless extraordinary devices or lost techniques shielded the workers and enabled construction.
rows.anchor: لا يتم إلا بأمر إلهي خارج عن العادة كصرف تأثير حرارة النار العظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another construction account says interlocking iron hooks joined rocks, with molten copper filling their cavities.
rows.anchor: كان بناؤه من الصخور مرتبطا بعضها ببعض بكلاليب من حديد

rows.speaker: أبو بكرة الشفي
rows.claim: A man told the Prophet he had seen the barrier and described alternating black and red stripes; the author takes the vision as probably physical, if the report is sound.
rows.anchor: يا رسول الله قد رأيت سد يأجوج ومأجوج قال : انعته لي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He doubts the story that al-Wathiq sent Sallam the Interpreter north to find the wall, calling it a lie because it conflicts with the Qurʾanic description.
rows.anchor: على تضعيفه وعندي أنه كذب لما فيه مما تأبى عنه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fuller “they were able” form, with its extra tāʾ in the clause about boring, is a subtle rhetorical choice.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى لطف الاتيان بالتاء في استطاعوا هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu’l-Qarnayn calls the completed wall a mercy from God, meaning the effect of great mercy for all people, especially its neighbors; if the reference is to his ability, that ability enables the mercy.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي ظهر على يدي وحصل بمباشرتي من السد الذي شأنه ما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His wording implies a divine favor beyond ordinary human workmanship, and “my Lord” reinforces the sense of mercy; Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads the demonstrative in feminine form.
rows.anchor: وفي الأخبار عنه بما ذكر إيذان على ما قيل بأنه ليس من قبيل الآثار

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: He reads “this” as feminine, either agreeing with the predicate or referring to the power and ability that built the wall.
rows.anchor: بتأنيث اسم الإشارة وخرج على أنه رعاية للخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “When my Lord’s promise comes” can mean its appointed time, with an omitted “time” and figurative attribution, or the promised event itself, without either figure.
rows.anchor: فالكلام على حذف مضاف والإسناد إلى الوعد مجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise is usually taken as the Day of Resurrection; the proposed specific reference to Gog and Magog’s emergence does not fit the syntax.
rows.anchor: والمراد من وقت ذلك يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coming promise includes its preliminary events, such as Gog and Magog, the Dajjal, and Jesus’s descent, not merely the nearness of its final occurrence.
rows.anchor: ما ينتظم مجيئه ومجيء مباديه من خروجهم وخروج الدجال ونزول عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dakkaʾ means level ground, with an implied feminine land; non-Kufis read dakkan as a verbal noun meaning flattened, or as an emphatic description, while Ibn ʿAtiyya’s “create” is rejected.
rows.anchor: بألف التأنيث الممدودة والموصوف مؤنث مقدر أي أرضا مستوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall will be flattened when some precursors to the promised time arrive, showing God’s power after the preceding account of mercy.
rows.anchor: وهذا الجعل وقت مجيء الوعد بمجيء بعض مباديه وفيه بيان لعظم قدرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu’l-Qarnayn may have inferred the promise from knowledge that mountains must be crushed at the Hour, or learned it from contemporary prophets; the timing of Gog and Magog may be prophecy or inference.
rows.anchor: واستفادته العلم بمجيئها ممن كان في عصره من الأنبياء عليهم السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ezekiel describes Gog and Magog’s end-time arrival from the north in countless peoples, their corruption and approach to Jerusalem, and their final destruction; if Dhu’l-Qarnayn was Alexander, he could have known this prophecy.
rows.anchor: وفي كتاب حزقيال عليه السلام الأخبار بمجيئهم في آخر الزمان من آخر الجربياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narration implies the barrier endures until the end times, when the promised time arrives and God levels it.
rows.anchor: أي وهو يستمر إلى آخر الزمان فإذا جاء وعد ربي جعله دكاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “My Lord’s promise is true” closes Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s story and confirms that the specified promise—and, more broadly, every divine promise—will certainly occur.
rows.anchor: أي وعده سبحانه المعهود أو كل ما وعد عز وجل به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural pronoun refers to creatures; “left” here can mean “made,” and the clause joins the account of the wall being flattened to confirm its fulfillment.
rows.anchor: للخلائق والترك بمعنى الجعل وهو من الأضداد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The crowding and mixing are like waves, with humans and jinn in turmoil from terror; this may describe great events before the first blast.
rows.anchor: يضطربون اضطراب البحر يختلط إنسهم وجنهم من شدة الهول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative reading makes people surge amid fear of Gog and Magog, or crowd around the completed wall in amazement; the author finds these interpretations strained.
rows.anchor: والمراد وجعلنا بعض الناس يوم إذ تم السد يموج في بعضهم للنظر إليه

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers that Gog and Magog themselves surge out of the barrier and crowd through the lands after Jesus descends.
rows.anchor: الأظهر كون الضمير ليأجوج ومأجوج أي وتركنا بعض يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
rows.claim: A sound Muslim report recounts that after Jesus kills the Dajjal, God tells him Gog and Magog have emerged; they drain waters, besiege believers at Mount Tur, then die by a divinely sent pestilence.
rows.anchor: في صحيح مسلم من حديث النواس بن سمعان بعد ذكر الدجال وهلاكه بباب لد

rows.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
rows.claim: In a Muslim narration, Gog and Magog boast that they have killed earth’s inhabitants and will attack heaven; their arrows return bloodied, then worms kill them all at once.
rows.anchor: لقد قتلنا من في الأرض هلم نقتل من في السماء فيرمون نشابهم إلى السماء

rows.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
rows.claim: A volunteer verifies their death; Muslims find the enemy piled together, and livestock feed on their corpses.
rows.anchor: فيتجرد رجل منهم محتسبا نفسه قد وطنها على أنه مقتول فينزل فيجدهم موتى

rows.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
rows.claim: Their stench covers the land; Jesus and his companions pray, and birds carry the corpses away, with reports differing on their destination.
rows.anchor: فيستغيثون بالله تعالى فيبعث الله سبحانه ريحا يمانية غبراء

rows.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
rows.claim: Rain cleans the earth and restores its bounty; a pomegranate feeds a group and milk animals provide abundantly, after which Muslims use Gog and Magog’s weapons for seven years.
rows.anchor: ثم يرسل الله عز وجل مطرا لا يكن منه بيت مدر ولا وبر فيغسل الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report demonstrates their great numbers; Ibn Hibban’s marfuʿ report from Ibn Masʿud says each leaves at least a thousand offspring, which some interpret as longevity.
rows.anchor: أن يأجوج ومأجوج أقل ما يترك أحدهم من صلبه ألفا من الذرية

rows.speaker: مكحول
rows.claim: Makḥul’s report that Gog and Magog occupy eighty of the world’s hundred years and comprise two distinct peoples of four hundred thousand each is false.
rows.anchor: قول مكحول الأرض مسيرة مائة عام ثمانون منها يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: The report assigning six of the world’s seven regions to Gog and Magog is dismissed as ignorant of geography.
rows.anchor: عن أبي الشيخ عن أبي أمامة الدنيا سبعة أقاليم

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report graded authentic by al-Hakim says God divided humanity into ten parts, nine being Gog and Magog; the author has not seen another scholar authenticate it.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى جزأ الإنس عشرة أجزاء فتسعة منهم يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gog and Magog are not the Tatars, despite their evident resemblance in destructive history.
rows.anchor: بطلان ما يزعمه بعض الناس من أنهم التاتار الذين أكثروا الفساد في البلاد

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: The trumpet is probably the second blast, fitting the resurrection context; the first blast is a general catastrophe, though another view avoids separating the two eras’ terrors.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن المراد النفخة الثانية لأنه المناسب لما بعد

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: A sound Prophetic report describes the horn-blower with the trumpet at his lips, brow bent, and ear cocked while awaiting the command.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كيف أنعم وقد التقم صاحب القرن القرن

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda says ṣūr means plural “images,” supported by a reading with an open wāw, but the author says the horn meaning is clear.
rows.anchor: أنه جمع صورة وأيد بقراءة الحسن

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abu al-Haytham compares denying the horn to denying the Throne, bridge, and balance; the nations agree that Israfil blows it.
rows.anchor: من أنكر أن يكون الصور قرنا فهو كمن أنكر العرش والصراط والميزان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gathers all creatures after their bodies have been reassembled on one plain for judgment and recompense, in a gathering beyond comprehension.
rows.anchor: أي الخلائق بعد ما تفرقت أوصالهم وتمزقت أجسادهم في صعيد واحد للحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God exposes Hell so the gathered can see it and hear its groaning; the terrifying display is especially directed at unbelievers even though everyone sees it.
rows.anchor: حيث جعلناها بحيث يرونها ويسمعون لها تغيظا وزفيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The display is dreadful and beyond measure, and Hell is assigned specifically to the unbelievers’ punishment.
rows.anchor: عرضا فظيعا هائلا لا يقادر قدره وتخصيص العرض بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their eyes were enveloped in a thick veil against the signs that lead reflective observers to remember and glorify God; “remembrance” figuratively names its cause, the signs.
rows.anchor: عن الآيات المؤدية لأولي الأبصار المتدبرين فيها إلى ذكري بالتوحيد والتمجيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “eyes” may mean inner sight, and remembrance may mean proper remembrance of God, His revelation to prophets, or specifically the Qurʾan.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون المراد بالأعين البصائر القلبية والمعنى كانت بصائرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplying “signs of My remembrance” by ellipsis is not the best account; the metaphor already explains why their sight is as if absent.
rows.anchor: الكلام على حذف مضاف أي عن آيات ذكري وليس بذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic statement that they could not hear portrays them as wholly deaf, deliberately turning from guidance, parallel to their blindness toward visible signs.
rows.anchor: نفي لسماعهم على أتم وجه ولذا عدل عن وكانوا صما الأخصر إليه

rows.speaker: ابن هشام
rows.claim: Ibn Hisham says an ellipsis must match its expressed verbal evidence in meaning; “Zayd strikes, and Amr” cannot omit “strikes” if it would mean “travels.”
rows.anchor: إن الدليل اللفظي لا بد من مطابقته للمحذوف معنى فلا يصح زيد ضارب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A grammarian instead derives the omitted remembrance from “hearing,” not the preceding mention; the author says that objection concerns readings where remembrance means Qurʾan or divine law.
rows.anchor: إن تقدير ذلك إنما هو بقرينة قوله تعالى سمعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause modifies or explains “the unbelievers,” condemning them and indicating why Hell was displayed to them.
rows.anchor: والموصول نعت الكافرين أو بدل منه أو بيان جيء به لذمهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative is a rebuke of unbelievers who suppose they can take God’s servants as protectors or objects of worship apart from Him.
rows.anchor: والهمزة للإنكار والتوبيخ على معنى إنكار الواقع واستقباحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “My servants” most likely includes angels, Jesus, and other honored beings; Qatada restricts it to angels, while Ibn ʿAbbas says devils and Muqatil says idols, both less convincing.
rows.anchor: والظاهر إرادة ما يعمهم وغيرهم ممن ذكرنا واختاره أبو حيان وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others take “My servants” to include the listed beings, idols, and other false objects of worship; the possessive may mark God’s ownership rather than honorific.
rows.anchor: أن يراد ما يعم المذكورين والأصنام وسائر المعبودات الباطلة من الكواكب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alleged allies may be objects of worship or supporters against God’s punishment; the clause may itself fill both complements of “suppose.”
rows.anchor: أي معبودين أو أنصارا لهم من بأسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis says real alliance would require reciprocity, which the worshipped beings deny; another makes the clause the first complement and omits the second, such as “beneficial,” but the author prefers rejecting the premise itself.
rows.anchor: لما أنه إنما يكون من الجانبين والمتخذون بمعزل عن ولايتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted second complement analysis is criticized for conceding their act of taking allies and granting it some standing.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن فيه تسليما لنفس الاتخاذ واعتدادا به في الجملة

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf links their presumption to their blindness and deafness: the added interrogative rebukes them again and stresses the independent blame of their belief.
rows.anchor: معطوف على كانت وكانوا دلالة على أن الحسبان ناشيء

rows.speaker: إرشاد العقل السليم
rows.claim: The Irshad objects that the explicit “unbelievers” needlessly replaces a pronoun, presumption is a different trait, and their old belief cannot be caused by their refusal to hear revelation; the author leaves the objection for reflection.
rows.anchor: أنه يأبى ذلك ترك الإضمار والتعرض لوصف آخر غير التعامي والتصام

rows.speaker: علي وزيد بن علي ومجاهد وعكرمة وقتادة وابن كثير ويعقوب
rows.claim: They read the phrase as “Is their sufficiency…,” with ḥasb as a noun meaning enough; taking God’s servants as allies is treated as their entire provision for judgment.
rows.anchor: بإسكان السين وضم الباء مضافا إلى الذين وخرج عن ذلك على أن حسب مبتدأ

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari makes the infinitive clause the subject of ḥasiba, since the interrogative makes the active participle operate like a verb.
rows.anchor: جعل الزمخشري المصدر المتحصل من أن والفعل فاعلا لحسب

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan objects that this verbal government applies to an explicit adjective, but the author answers that Sibawayh permits raising subjects after comparable interpreted adjectives.
rows.anchor: واعترض عليه أبو حيان بأن حسب مؤول باسم الفاعل

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: They read nazulan with a still zāy.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو حيوة وأبو عمرو بخلاف عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” introduces the outcome of their disbelief and other destructive deeds; it may be an omitted subject with the following clause explanatory, or a subject followed by a predicate and apposition.
rows.anchor: بيان لمآل كفرهم وسائر معاصيهم إثر بيان أعمالهم المحبطة بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other grammatical parses make “that” the subject, “their recompense” its apposition or predicate, and Hell the predicate or explanatory apposition; the referent may be the punishment or their sins.
rows.anchor: بدل منه بدل اشتمال أو بدل كل من كل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A parse that treats the following sentence as predicate requires an omitted return pronoun; the author questions it because such deletion is normally licensed by partitive, locative, or repeated-preposition constructions.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن العائد المجرور إنما يكثر حذفه في مثل ذلك إذا جر بحرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “for what they disbelieved” links the punishment to their disbelief and to mocking God’s signs and messengers; it may attach directly to recompense despite intervening Hell.
rows.anchor: أي مهزوأ بهما فإنهم لم يقنعوا بمجرد الكفر بالآيات والرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Signs” may specifically mean the miracles shown through the messengers and the scriptures sent down to them; making the clause independent is less apparent.
rows.anchor: المعجزات الظاهرة على أيدي الرسل عليهم السلام والصحف الإلهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers’ promise contrasts with the preceding warning: their faith in God’s signs and meeting Him, with righteous deeds, determines their promised end.
rows.anchor: بيان بطريق الوعد لمآل الذين اتصفوا بأضداد ما اتصف به الكفرة

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: The past tense in “were theirs” reflects God’s prior decree and hints that mercy reaches believers from eternal grace, unlike Hell’s preparation in response to later bad choices.
rows.anchor: فالمضى باعتبار ما ذكر وفيه على ما قال شيخ الإسلام إيماء إلى أن أثر الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past may also mark the promised reward as certain; saying the gardens “were theirs” conveys certainty more strongly than saying they were prepared.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون ما وعدوا به لتحققه نزل منزلة الماضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike a prepared object, the gardens keep increasing; reports say a tree is planted for a believer for every glorification, a further subtlety in the wording.
rows.anchor: فإن اعتاد الشيء وتهيئته يقتضي تمامية أمره وكماله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Firdaus means “garden” in Roman speech.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد أن الفردوس هو البستان بالرومية

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says it means vineyard in Nabataean and gives its source form as firdasa.
rows.anchor: عن السدي أنه الكرم بالنبطية وأصله فرداسا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas asked Kaʿb, who said it means a grape garden in Syriac; ʿIkrima says it means “garden” in Ethiopic.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن الحرث أن ابن عباس سأل كعبا عن الفردوس

rows.speaker: القفال والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal describes a garden thick with trees; al-Zajjaj says it can mean valleys where varied plants grow.
rows.anchor: هي الجنة الملتفة بالأشجار وحكى الزجاج أنها الأودية التي تنبت ضروبا

rows.speaker: المبرد والفراء
rows.claim: They treat Firdaus as Arabic for an interwoven garden, especially one with vines; al-Farraʾ says it may be masculine or feminine.
rows.anchor: الشجر الملتف والأغلب عليه العنب ونص الفراء على أنه عربي أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that the word occurs in Arabic only in Hassan’s verse is false: Umayya, Jarir, and a pre-Islamic Meccan caller also used it.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أنها لم تسمع في كلام العرب إلا في قول حسان

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet says to ask God for Firdaus, the middle and highest Garden beneath the Throne from which the rivers flow.
rows.anchor: إذا سألتم الله تعالى فاسألوه الفردوس فإنه وسط الجنة وأعلى الجنة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة بن الجراح وكعب
rows.claim: A marfuʿ report gives Paradise one hundred levels and calls Firdaus its highest; Kaʿb says nothing in Paradise is higher, and other reports describe its inhabitants hearing the Throne.
rows.anchor: الجنة مائة درجة ما بين كل درجتين ما بين السماء والأرض والفردوس أعلى الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan’s reading of gardens around Firdaus still fails because the verse would then place all believers there, although some are in Firdaus itself.
rows.anchor: هذا لا يشفي الغليل لما أن الآية حينئذ تفيد أن جميع المؤمنين في جنات حول الفردوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author favors taking Firdaus in the reports in one sense and in this verse in another, choosing a meaning such as thickly interwoven trees that fits the poetry.
rows.anchor: أن الفردوس في الآثار بمعنى وفي الآية بمعنى آخر وتختار من معانيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to ask for Firdaus does not conflict with asking for the Prophet alone to receive al-Wasila: one grade may contain levels, with al-Wasila its highest level.
rows.anchor: لا مانع من انقسام الدرجة الواحدة إلى درجات بعضها أعلى من بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reconciliation makes the Prophet’s “degree” a rank of status while Firdaus is a spatial grade.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد من الدرجة في حديث الوسيلة درجة المكانة لا المكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “for them” may modify an omitted circumstantial or explanatory expression; nazulan can be the predicate of “were” or a circumstantial description.
rows.anchor: على أنه حال من قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If nuzul means a welcome for a guest, the gardens’ fruits are their welcome—or the gardens themselves are an emphatic welcome, hinting that they are modest beside God’s promised gifts.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى كانت لهم ثمار جنات الفردوس نزلا أو جعلت نفس الجنات نزلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If nuzul means lodging, the phrase simply means that the gardens are their dwelling.
rows.anchor: وإن جعلت بمعنى المنزل فالمعنى ظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Abiding” is an accusative circumstantial phrase, either estimated or concurrent; it is concurrent because their being in Paradise has no endpoint.
rows.anchor: نصب على الحالية وهي مقدرة عند البعض وحقق أنها حال مقارنة

rows.speaker: ابن عيسى
rows.claim: Ibn ʿIsa and others take hawlan as a verbal noun meaning a change or movement; believers seek no change from Paradise because nothing is better, despite differing ranks.
rows.anchor: هو كما قال ابن عيسى وغيره مصدر كالعوج والصغر والعود

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya suggests a collective noun whose singular is hawala; the author considers this remote.
rows.anchor: كأنه اسم جمع وكأن واحده حوالة ولا يخفى بعده

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: A view transmitted by al-Zajjaj makes the word mean a device for changing places, which the author calls weak and strained.
rows.anchor: هو بمعنى الحيلة في التنقل وهو ضعيف متكلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lack of desire to leave can reinforce eternal residence: with no compulsion and no wish to depart, no outcome remains except abiding; the wording also implies no boredom.
rows.anchor: إذا لم يريدوا الانتقال لا ينتقلون لعدم الإكراه فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attached clause may be circumstantial from those abiding or nested within that circumstance.
rows.anchor: والجملة حال من صاحب خالدين أو من ضميره فيه فتكون حالا متداخلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sea means the entire kind of sea; ink originally denotes anything that extends something and conventionally means a pen’s ink. God’s words mean His knowledge and wisdom, which have no end.
rows.anchor: هو في الأصل اسم لكل ما يمد به الشيء واختص في العرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even a vast sea would run out before God’s inexhaustible words; finite quantities remain finite when another like them is added.
rows.anchor: مع كثرته ولم يبق منه شيء لتناهيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final clause is divine speech added to confirm the preceding statement, with an omitted parallel conditional clause understood from the expressed one.
rows.anchor: وهذا كلام من جهته تعالى شأنه غير داخل في الكلام الملقن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “before God’s words run out” does not imply their eventual exhaustion; the sea ends while the words remain, and the wording also pairs the clauses.
rows.anchor: للدلالة على أن ثم نفادا في الجملة محققا أو مقدرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any number of imagined additional seas would still be finite; this is more general than the comparison with seven seas, though that specific number evokes popular speech and adds vividness.
rows.anchor: والمثل للجنس شائع على أمثال كثيرة تفرض كل منها مددا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated wording “sea” and “words,” and the relation of the Lord to the Prophet in “my Lord,” reinforce the statement and honor its addressee.
rows.anchor: وفي إضافة الكلمات إلى اسم الرب المضاف إلى ضميره صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madadan is accusative as a specification, supported by a poetic line; Abu al-Fadl al-Razi instead parses it as a cognate object meaning “with an extension,” an analysis the author calls strained.
rows.anchor: على التمييز كما في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reference to seven seas adds a rhetorical point and evokes the familiar popular image of seven seas used for an unreachable quantity, without limiting the number of possible supplies.
rows.anchor: وذلك أبلغ من وجه آخر وهو ما في تخصيص هذا العدد من النكتة

rows.speaker: الأعرج
rows.claim: Al-Aʿraj reads madadan with kasra on mīm as the plural of muddah, the supply of ink a writer uses.
rows.anchor: بكسر الميم على أنه جمع مدة وهو ما يستمده الكاتب

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والأعمش والتيمي وابن محيصن وحميد والحسن وأبو عمرو وحفص
rows.claim: They read midādan with an alif, meaning ink or writing supply.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والأعمش بخلاف والتيمي وابن محيصن

rows.speaker: حي بن أخطب
rows.claim: As a reported occasion of revelation, Huyayy ibn Akhtab alleges contradiction between the Qurʾan’s “much good” from wisdom and its “little knowledge”; the author says quantity is relative and finite learning is little beside God’s words.
rows.anchor: أن حي بن أخطب كما رواه الترمذي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed occasion is that Jews challenged the Prophet’s universal mission and knowledge because he did not explain the soul; the answer is that knowing its essence is not needed for prophetic religion.
rows.anchor: كيف تزعم أنك نبي الأمم كلها ومبعوث إليها وأنك أعطيت من العلم ما يحتاجه الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That second occasion is not answered by this verse alone; it needs the following verse, and the claim that prophets know everything people need is not implied by their mission.
rows.anchor: أن الآية لا تكون جوابا عما ذكر على تقدير صحة كون ذلك سبب النزول إلا بضم الآية الآتية
